items.title: Hashing is one-way; encryption is reversible
items.claim: A password manager stores user passwords. Which approach is appropriate?

options.text: Store a salted hash (using bcrypt, scrypt or argon2) — passwords cannot be recovered from the hash, only verified by re-hashing user input. Encryption would be wrong here because no system needs to recover the plaintext
Encrypt with the user's password as the key

items.reveal_title: Hash for verification, encrypt for transmission
items.reveal:
Common confusion: hashing is one-way (no key, no recovery); encryption is two-way (with a key, recoverable). For password storage, you only need to verify; hashing fits.

Password-specific hash functions (bcrypt 1999, scrypt 2009, Argon2 2015 — the Password Hashing Competition winner) are deliberately slow and memory-hard to resist brute-force attacks. The 2012 LinkedIn breach exposed 6.5m unsalted SHA-1 password hashes; a third were cracked within days.
items.why: Choosing the right cryptographic primitive matters more than choosing a strong one. SHA-256 is strong; using it for passwords (without proper KDF) is still wrong.

items.title: RAM is volatile; storage persists
items.claim: A computer is suddenly unplugged mid-operation. What happens to data?

options.text: Data in RAM is lost (DRAM needs refresh to retain charge); data in SSD/HDD persists. This is why crash safety requires explicit flushing (fsync) to storage

items.reveal:
DRAM cells lose charge in milliseconds without refresh. SRAM (cache) holds state while powered but is volatile. SSDs (NAND flash) and HDDs are non-volatile.

Databases use write-ahead logging (WAL): changes go to log on disk before being applied to main data structures, so a crash mid-transaction can be replayed or rolled back. Filesystems (ext4, NTFS, APFS) use journaling for similar reasons. NVRAM and persistent memory (Intel Optane, discontinued 2022) blurred the boundary briefly.
items.why: The volatile/persistent distinction shapes everything from OS design to database recovery to backup strategy.

items.title: The first computer 'bug'
items.claim: In 1947 a literal insect was taped into a log book at Harvard. Who was the engineer most associated with the incident?
items.reveal_title: Grace Hopper's team at Harvard Mark II
items.reveal:
A moth was found jamming a relay in the Mark II computer on 9 September 1947 and taped into the log with the note 'First actual case of bug being found'.

The term 'bug' had been used in engineering since at least Edison.
items.why: Terminology often predates its famous origin story; jargon collects illustrative anecdotes.
